settings.hint: Settings — grid, welding, sampling quality and packing, which shape every texture rather than one of them. Currently {parts}
settings.reset_layout.tip: Put every panel back where it started. Nothing you have extracted is affected
settings.grid.cell_size.tip: The spacing everything snaps to and the grid is drawn at, in world pixels
settings.grid.snap: Snap marks and textures to it
settings.grid.snap.tip: Dragged positions and freshly extracted sizes land on cell boundaries, which is what keeps a packed sheet tidy
settings.grid.draw.tip: Show the grid behind the photo and the atlas
settings.weld_radius.tip: How near a dragged corner has to come to an existing one, in screen pixels, before it snaps exactly onto it. Two marks sharing a corner exactly is what makes their textures line up. Zero turns it off
settings.supersample.tip: Warp at a multiple of the output size and average down. This is what stops a slice taken at a steep angle from stair-stepping, and it costs the square of the setting in time
settings.supersample.1x: 1x — sample the photo once per texel
settings.supersample.note: Warps at a multiple of the output size and averages down, which is what keeps a slice taken at an angle from stair-stepping.
settings.padding.tip: Empty pixels left between slices when packing, so that filtering at a distance cannot pull one texture's colour into its neighbour
settings.power_of_two: Round the atlas to a power of two
settings.power_of_two.tip: Grow the exported sheet to the next power of two, which some engines and compressed formats still require
settings.export_maps: Write the PBR maps as well
settings.export_maps.tip: Atlas and Individually write the material's normal, roughness and occlusion beside the colour, as a zip. The maps are derived at full size for a file rather than at the resolution the panels preview them at, so this is slower than exporting the colour alone
settings.export_maps.note: A GLB always carries its maps; this is for the two flat exports.
settings.ai.tip: Depth estimation is the only one, and the only thing in this app that fetches anything. Off, no request is ever made, no model is downloaded, and depth is unavailable — everything else works as it always did
settings.ai.note: Used for one thing: estimating depth from a single photograph, so a mark's bow goes into the mesh and the normal map as something measured rather than guessed from shading. Runs in your browser; the runtime and about 100 MB of weights are fetched from jsDelivr once, when you first ask for depth.
settings.ai.rest: Nothing else here is AI. {flatten}, {pbr}, and the normal and occlusion maps taken from shading are arithmetic over your own pixels, offline, and keep working with this off.
settings.shortcuts.tip: Every keyboard shortcut and mouse gesture, and the licences of everything bundled into this file

atlas_bar.snap_edges.tip: Snap to the other slices: edges flush against edges and centres lined up with centres, which is what closes a gap the grid cannot
atlas_bar.snap_grid.tip: Snap to the grid: dragged positions land on cell boundaries, currently {size}px. The Settings menu has the size
atlas_bar.show_grid.tip: Draw the grid behind the sheet
atlas_bar.fit.tip: Frame the whole sheet. Double-clicking the canvas does the same
tiling_bar.cols.tip: How many copies across. More copies make a repeating feature obvious sooner than a single tile ever can
tiling_bar.wrap_repeat.tip: Repeat: every copy identical, so a seam shows up as a seam. This is what an engine does by default
tiling_bar.wrap_mirror.tip: Mirrored repeat: every other copy flipped, which hides any seam at the cost of obvious symmetry. Not every engine can do this
tiling_bar.seams.tip: Draw a line where one tile stops and the next starts, so a mismatch can be told apart from the texture's own detail
tiling_bar.fit.tip: Frame the whole tiled sheet. Double-clicking the canvas does the same
tiling_bar.summary.tip: The texture's size, and which edges have been welded to make it repeat
preview3d.viewport.tip: Drag to orbit, scroll or pinch to zoom, right-drag or two fingers to pan

preview3d.empty.select: Select a single texture to see it lit, or a photo to see the depth behind it.

preview3d.shape.plane.title: Plane — fitted to the texture
preview3d.shape.plane.tip: A plane at the texture's own aspect ratio. This is the fitting mesh: the shape that stands for the marked surface, and the only one relief reaches
preview3d.shape.box.title: Box — reads across a hard edge
preview3d.shape.box.tip: A box, for judging how the material reads around a hard edge
preview3d.shape.cylinder.title: Cylinder — wraps once, undistorted
preview3d.shape.cylinder.tip: A cylinder whose height comes from its own circumference, so a tiling texture wraps it exactly once without being stretched
preview3d.shape.sphere.title: Sphere — curvature everywhere
preview3d.shape.sphere.tip: A sphere, for curvature in every direction at once
measure.mode.hint_off: Draw a measurement or a material channel over every viewport. Painted over the Atlas, the photo and the tiling preview at once.
measure.mode.hint: {title} — {subtitle}. Painted over the Atlas, the photo and the tiling preview at once.
measure.overlay.tip: How strongly the overlay is painted over the texture underneath it
measure.numbers.on: Stop printing the readings on the map
measure.numbers.off: Print the readings themselves on the map
measure.numbers.correspond_off: Print each slice's name on it and on its mark
histogram.canvas.tip: How the texture's values are distributed, red green and blue over each other. The blue line is the mean.
histogram.canvas.tip_with_ref: How the texture's values are distributed, red green and blue over each other. The blue line is the mean. The white outline behind is the extraction before the lighting was flattened, so the effect of every setting is visible in place
histogram.canvas.tip_no_ref: How the texture's values are distributed, red green and blue over each other. The blue line is the mean. Flatten the lighting to see the before state drawn behind it
histogram.mean.tip: Average brightness. This is what an exposure target moves, and the blue line marks it
histogram.spread.tip: Standard deviation of brightness. Flattening usually lowers it, because a shadow across the surface was part of the spread
histogram.range.tip: The darkest and brightest values present
histogram.blown.tip: This much of the texture is at pure white, where the photograph kept no detail. Nothing here can recover it
histogram.cast.tip: How far the average colour is from neutral. A strong cast is usually the light rather than the surface — try neutralising it
dock.close_panel.tip: Close this panel. Nothing in it is lost — it can be reopened from the Panels menu

problems.overlap.title: {a} and {b} overlap
problems.overlap.detail: Both are drawn into the same pixels, so the exported atlas has them blended together. Move one, or press Pack to lay them all out again.
problems.waste.title: The atlas is {percent}% empty space
problems.waste.detail: It would export at {width} x {height}, and an export is charged for its bounding box, so the gaps cost memory exactly as the textures do. Press Pack to close them up.
problems.dirty.title_one: {count} mark has changed since the last extraction
problems.dirty.title_other: {count} marks have changed since the last extraction
problems.dirty.detail: The atlas is still showing the pixels these enclosed before. Press Extract, or Shift+R.
problems.names.title: {count} textures are called "{name}"
problems.names.detail: Exporting them individually will number the duplicates rather than overwrite them, so the files will not be named what you expect.
problems.orphan.title_one: {count} texture no longer has a mark
problems.orphan.title_other: {count} textures no longer have a mark
problems.orphan.detail: The pixels are safe and will still export, but there is nothing left to re-sample: lighting and tiling still work, local space and depth do not.
problems.coverage.title_one: {count} texture sampled past the edge of the photograph
problems.coverage.title_other: {count} textures sampled past the edge of the photograph
problems.coverage.detail: {name} is {percent}% transparent. The mark, or the area it was extended to in local space, reaches outside the image.

props.empty.multi_textures: {count} textures selected. Tiling and transform editing apply to a single selection.
props.empty.multi_marks: {count} marks selected. Local space and edge bend apply to a single selection.
props.empty.none: Select something to edit it: a texture in the Atlas, or a mark or a photo in the Source panel.
props.lens.title: Lens
props.lens.hint: Radial distortion from the camera that took this photograph. A lens bends the whole frame by one rule, so this belongs to the photograph rather than to any mark on it — set it once and all {count} mark{plural} here are sampled through it. Hover a mark to see the projected grid, which is the best thing on screen for judging it: get the correction right and the grid follows the mortar courses all the way across
props.lens.distortion.tip: Radial distortion. Negative is barrel — straight lines bowing outward, which is what a wide-angle lens does and by far the common case. Positive is pincushion. Zero leaves the photograph exactly as shot
props.lens.fine.tip: The fourth-order term, for the residual a single coefficient cannot reach — usually only needed on a very wide lens, and worth leaving at zero until the first slider has done what it can
props.lens.fit.tip: Solve for the coefficient that makes the {count} traced edge(s) on this photograph straightest
props.lens.fit.tip_none: Bend a mark's edge along something you know is straight — a mortar course, a window frame — and this can solve for the lens from it
props.lens.clear.tip: Back to the photograph exactly as it was shot
props.lens.report.need_bend: Bend a mark's edge along a line you know is straight first.
props.lens.report.already_straight: Those {count} edge(s) are already as straight as a radial correction can make them.
props.lens.report.fitted_one: Fitted k1 {k1} from {count} traced edge, {percent}% straighter.
props.lens.report.fitted_other: Fitted k1 {k1} from {count} traced edges, {percent}% straighter.
props.scene.title: Depth
props.scene.hint: Depth estimated for the whole photograph and unprojected through a pinhole camera, so the shape it recorded can be looked at. A diagnostic rather than a reconstruction: relative depth has no absolute scale or offset, and the camera settings below change the surface's slant and how far the background sits rather than bending anything. The model is not in this page — around 100 MB, fetched the first time it is asked for
props.scene.focal.tip: Neither this nor the shift below can bend a flat surface — they change its slant. Tune against angles you know, a room's corner or a floor; anything that stays curved is the model saying so
props.scene.shift.tip: How far the background sits behind the foreground
props.scene.trim.tip: A sky sits at one end of the depth range in a sliver of the pixels and squeezes everything nearer into the rest, so trimming it away is usually what makes an outdoor photo readable
props.scene.smoothing.tip: Blurs the depth map before it is unprojected, because noise in it reads as a surface that is rough where nothing is
props.scene_mesh.title: Mesh
props.scene_mesh.hint: The surface the depth was unprojected into: how it is shaded, how finely it is divided, and where it is torn rather than stretched
props.scene_mesh.display.tip: Normals colour the surface by which way it faces, which reads shape far better than the photograph does — the photo carries its own shading and hides the form it is draped on. Wireframe shows where triangles were dropped
props.scene_mesh.edge.tip: Neighbours further apart than this in depth get no triangle between them. Too high and every railing against the sky becomes a sheet stretching to the horizon; too low and the surface breaks into confetti
props.transform.title: Atlas transform
props.transform.hint: Where this slice sits on the atlas sheet, how large it is drawn there and which way round it is. None of it resamples the pixels — it is the arrangement, not the extraction, except for the two flips, which change the texture itself
props.transform.xy.tip: Where the slice sits on the atlas sheet, in sheet pixels
props.transform.scale.tip: How large it is drawn on the sheet. This does not resample the pixels — extend the mark in Local space to gain real detail
props.transform.rotation.tip: Turn the slice on the sheet, in degrees. Packing ignores rotation
props.transform.rotate_left.tip: Turn a quarter turn anticlockwise  (Left arrow)
props.transform.rotate_right.tip: Turn a quarter turn clockwise  (Right arrow)
props.transform.flip_x.tip: Mirror the pixels left to right. This changes the texture itself, so it is what gets exported — not just how it is shown  (Shift+X)
props.transform.flip_y.tip: Mirror the pixels top to bottom, in the exported texture as well as on screen  (Shift+Y)
props.transform.reset.tip: Put position, scale and rotation back to what the extraction gave it
props.local.title: Local space
props.local.hint: What area of the photograph the mark samples, measured along the flattened surface rather than in the photo. Extending it takes the extra pixels from the photograph in perspective rather than stretching the ones already here; holding Alt in the Atlas panel drags the same values
props.local.orphan: This texture is no longer tied to a mark, so there is nothing left to re-sample. Local space edits the marked surface, not the extracted pixels.
props.local.extend.tip: Push the {side} edge out past the mark, as a percentage of the marked width. The extra is sampled along the surface in perspective, not stretched out of the pixels already here. Negative trims instead. {state}
props.local.bend: Edge bend: {values}%. Each edge has two Bézier handles on the mark: drag both the same way to bow it, opposite ways to S-curve it.
props.local.bend.tip: How far the middle of each edge sits off its chord. Zero on all four means the mark is a flat quad — though an S-bent edge reads zero here too, because its middle really is back on the line
props.local.reset.tip: Sample exactly the marked quad again: no extension, no bend
props.local.reset.tip_already: The sampled area is already exactly the marked quad
props.local.rectify.tip: Straighten the whole photograph through this mark, as a new one. Everything on the same flat surface comes back square with it, so the rest of the wall can then be marked with quads that really are rectangles. Anything not on that surface — foreground, a wall at another angle — is sheared instead, and the far side of the plane's horizon cannot come through at all
props.lighting.title: Lighting
props.lighting.hint: A photo has the light baked in and the engine will light the surface again, so flattening estimates that illumination and divides it out — leaving the albedo, the flat shadowless look of an overcast day. The Atlas and the tiling preview show the result as it will be exported, as you change it
props.lighting.mode.off.tip: Export the pixels with the light they were photographed under
props.lighting.mode.gradient.tip: Fit one smooth surface to the illumination and divide it out. Cannot mistake an albedo edge for a shadow, so it is the safe one
props.lighting.mode.local.tip: Follow the illumination locally, which lifts a shadow with an edge to it — at the risk of flattening large real features
props.lighting.amount.tip: How much of the estimated illumination to divide out. Short of 100% keeps some of the original modelling, which can read better than a perfectly flat albedo
props.lighting.radius.tip: How far the estimate looks for the local light level, as a fraction of the texture. Smaller removes more shadow and starts eating the texture's own large features
props.lighting.falloff.tip: How much the fitted surface is allowed to bend: linear is a straight ramp across the texture, complex can follow a pool of light in the middle of it
props.lighting.per_channel.tip: Estimate the light separately per channel, so a warm lamp on one side and daylight on the other both come out
props.lighting.balance.tip: Push the average towards grey. Assumes the surface really is neutral on average — a genuinely coloured one gets drained
props.lighting.match_to.tip: Scale the result to a common mean brightness, so textures cut from different photographs sit together instead of each keeping its own exposure. At zero the brightness is left as shot
props.lighting.extract_shading.tip: Add the illumination that was divided out to the atlas as its own texture: mid grey is unchanged, darker was in shadow
props.material.title: Material
props.material.hint: How the surface responds to light, and the maps that carry it. Everything below Generate PBR is inferred from the colour rather than measured — the sliders are here to argue with it. The 3D panel is where the result is judged, and clicking one of the thumbnails puts that map on every viewport
props.material.roughness.tip: How much the surface scatters light. 0 is a mirror, 1 is chalk
props.material.roughness.tip_mapped: The level the generated roughness map varies around
props.material.metalness.tip: Whether the surface is a metal. Almost nothing photographed as a surface texture is, and a value between 0 and 1 is not a real material at all
props.material.relief.tip: How far to believe the flattened-out lighting about the shape of the surface. Bright is read as standing proud, dark as sitting in a recess. Zero exports a flat normal map
props.material.occlusion.tip: How much of the shadow that was divided out to hand back through the occlusion channel. This is the one derivation here that is measured rather than guessed
props.material.generate_pbr.tip: Read this texture and infer a normal, roughness and cavity map from its colour, setting all three strengths from what it finds. Works with the lighting left in, unlike Relief and Occlusion above
props.material.clear.tip: Drop the colour-derived maps and go back to the albedo with only what the lighting gave
props.material.fine_relief.tip: Pixel-scale relief taken from the high-frequency part of the colour — grain, mortar lines, chipping. Large dark patches are deliberately excluded, so paint does not become a trench
props.material.roughness_map.tip: How far roughness is allowed to vary from the level above. Areas broken up at pixel scale read rougher; blown-out highlights read smoother. Zero exports a single roughness value
props.material.cavity.tip: Darken wherever the colour is below its local average, on the reasoning that a recess is dark because less light reaches it. This channel only ever darkens
props.material.channel.colour.tip: The base colour, exactly as it will be exported — tiled and, if the lighting was flattened, with that lighting taken out. Click to clear the overlay and see it on its own
props.material.channel.normal.tip: Tangent-space normals, +Y up, as glTF asks for. Flat is the pale lilac; anything else is relief the shading or the colour implied. Click to see it full size in every panel
props.material.channel.roughness.tip: Light is rough, dark is smooth. Uniform grey means the map is doing nothing the plain roughness value could not. Click to see it full size in every panel
props.material.channel.occlusion.tip: White is open, dark is a recess ambient light does not reach. Read from the red channel, and it only ever darkens. Click to see it full size in every panel
props.tiling.title: Seamless tiling
props.tiling.hint: Cross-fading opposite edges so they match exactly and the texture repeats without a join. It costs detail in the band it touches, so an edge that never meets another copy is better left alone. Applies to what is displayed and to both export paths
props.tiling.mode.off.tip: Export exactly what was extracted. Any seam stays a seam
props.tiling.mode.auto.tip: Cross-fade opposite edges so they match exactly and the texture repeats without a join. Applies to the preview and both exports
props.tiling.which_edges.tip: A skirting board that only ever runs sideways wants X; a pipe or a column wants Y. Welding an edge that never meets another copy spends detail for nothing
props.tiling.both.tip: Weld all four edges: the texture repeats in every direction
props.tiling.x.tip: Weld left to right only, leaving the top and bottom edges their full detail. What a run of skirting or a frieze wants
props.tiling.y.tip: Weld top to bottom only, leaving the sides their full detail. What a pipe or a column wants
props.tiling.blend.tip: How wide the cross-fade is, as a fraction of the texture. Wider hides a bigger mismatch and costs detail across that whole band
props.tiling.mirror_2x2.tip: Make a new texture four times the area, mirrored about both axes. It tiles perfectly by construction, at the cost of visible symmetry. A new texture rather than a change to this one, since it doubles both dimensions
props.depth.title: Depth
props.depth.hint: Depth is estimated for the whole photograph, sampled through this mark, and the plane the flattening already assumed is subtracted out. What is left is how far the surface bowed away from flat, and it becomes the shape of the mesh in the 3D panel and in an exported model. The model is not in this page — around 100 MB, fetched once
props.depth.orphan: This texture's mark is gone, so there is nothing to sample depth along.
props.depth.awaiting_extract: The mesh and the normal map this shapes belong to an extracted texture, so these settings will take effect once this mark has been extracted.
props.depth.estimate.tip: Fetch the depth model (around 100 MB, once) and estimate depth for this photograph. Later imports then estimate themselves
props.depth.use.tip: Shape the mesh and the normal map with the depth measured for this photograph, instead of treating the surface as flat. It is the one normal input that is measured rather than inferred from the photograph's own shading
props.depth.bow.tip: How much of the measured bow to put into the mesh itself. Relative depth carries no scale, so this is a judgement. Only the plane shape takes it
props.depth.in_normal.tip: The same relief in the normal map instead of the mesh, for an engine that wants a flat quad. It adds to the relief inferred from the shading rather than replacing it, since it carries the low-frequency shape that inference is worst at
props.depth.subdivision.tip: {n}×{n} quads across the plane, in the preview and in an exported model. Finer follows the bow more closely
props.depth.flatness: This surface sat {percent}% of the scene's depth range off the plane it was flattened onto.
props.depth.extract_to_measure: Extract this mark to measure how far its surface stood off the flat plane.
tiling.empty.one: Select a single texture to preview its tiling
tiling.empty.none: Select a texture in the atlas to preview its tiling
mark.notice.bad_quad: Those four points do not form a usable quad
mark.notice.no_images: No supported image files in that selection
depth.error.ai_off: AI features are off, so depth is unavailable. Settings has the switch.
depth.error.no_runtime: this browser cannot run the depth model
depth.error.no_file: that photograph has no stored file to read
settings.language.tip: Follow the browser, or pick a language to remember
